source.abstract: Photonic parallel computing inspires important approaches to artificial intelligence, promising substantial gains in processing speed, energy efficiency, and latency. Nevertheless, the integration density and robustness of most optical computing architectures continue to pose significant challenges. Here, we report a waveguide-array optical neural network based on thin-film lithium niobate (TFLN). By virtue of the compact size of the waveguide arrays, this architecture yields a computational density of 9.48×104 TOPS/mm2. Moreover, the high-speed and energy-efficient characteristics of the TFLN platform enable a computing speed of 135.6 TOPS with an energy efficiency of 6.28 TOPS/W. Our experiments on the iris flower and handwritten digit recognition demonstrate accuracies of 100% and 89.7%, respectively. The device achieves over 90% accuracy across a 75-nm operating bandwidth in the iris flower recognition task, indicating the wavelength insensitivity and superior robustness of the waveguide array. As a compact paradigm for optical neural networks, we demonstrate the potential of waveguide arrays in performing optical computation, thereby offering solutions for the advancement of edge computing, optoelectronic integration, and intelligent automation.
source.title: Waveguide-array optical neural network on thin-film lithium niobate platform

source.abstract: Abstract Optical computing encodes and processes information through the continuous evolution of optical fields, whereas digital electronic systems operate on discrete logical states. Conventional optical-to-electronic interfaces convert measured optical responses into electronically accessible data, with task-specific interpretation subsequently performed in the electronic domain. Here, we introduce and experimentally validate a proof-of-concept light-field-to-bits (LFB) computing architecture that maps information-bearing light fields onto predefined 4-bit codewords. The proposed architecture comprises two cascaded diffractive layers that route optical energy at the output plane into eight predefined regions of interest (ROIs) arranged as four differential pairs, with each pair encoding one bit through relative-intensity comparison. We physically implement the first diffractive layer and computationally emulate the second, using a CMOS sensor to capture the intermediate intensity distribution. We further develop a differentiable physics-assisted surrogate model within a camera-in-the-loop framework. The experimental prototype achieves 4-bit codeword accuracies of 95.31% for geometrically perturbed hexadecimal inputs and 93.36% for traffic-sign inputs subjected to combined viewpoint distortion and noise. Meanwhile, the optical front-end exploits the intrinsic parallelism of diffractive propagation, performing high-dimensional optical transformations equivalent to ∼51.2 Giga-Operations (GOPs) of multiply accumulate (MAC) operations within a ∼1.16 ns optical time-of-flight, while the electronic stage only performs lightweight spatial aggregation at the scale of tens of Mega-FLOPs. This strategy establishes the feasibility of LFB computing as an interface between continuous optical information processing and discrete digital decision-making for latency-sensitive machine vision and edge sensing.
source.title: Light-Field-to-Bits Computing via an Online-Trainable Cascaded Optoelectronic Neural Network

source.abstract: Phase-only optical neural networks (ONNs) promise energy-efficient inference through passive photonic components. Two gaps separate continuous-valued simulation from hardware deployment: commercial phase light modulators (PLMs) realize only discrete phase levels, and mechanical mounting fixes the propagation distance that training treats as a learnable parameter. The physics-aware simulation platform presented in1 is extended with quantization-aware training (QAT) over three phase encodings and a propagation-distance sensitivity analysis that holds trained phase masks fixed. Across the configurations tested, 4-bit resolution is the point where accuracy stabilizes and approaches the continuous-phase baseline, while the lowest bit depths collapse. The distance analysis bounds usable mounting tolerance to a few millimeters around the trained optimum. These results give hardware specifications for laboratory testbed implementation of discrete-phase optical inference.
